description:
No sample of honey recovered from an Egyptian tomb has ever been proven genuine and edible; every claimed case has turned out to be a different substance, or only a trace residue. This comes from honey's own reference literature, which flags the claim as a persistent myth.

The real record is older than the myth anyway, and it was not found in Egypt. Real, confirmed honey residue has been recovered elsewhere, and it predates the Tutankhamun story by thousands of years.

the age of the oldest confirmed honey remains ever found: residue on the inside of clay jars, in a tomb in the country of Georgia.

Honey really does resist spoiling, just not by magic. Bees mix an enzyme into the nectar they carry that produces gluconic acid and hydrogen peroxide, both of which stop bacteria growing, and its low moisture content does the rest. It only stays stable sealed and dry. Exposed to damp air, it will eventually ferment like anything else.

Ancient Georgians took the idea further than anyone: several types of honey, linden, berry, and meadow-flower, were buried alongside the dead as provisions for the journey to the afterlife.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honey: states plainly that no edible honey has been found in Egyptian tombs, that all such claimed cases have proven to be other substances or only chemical traces, explains honey's real preservation chemistry (bee-derived glucose oxidase producing gluconic acid and hydrogen peroxide, plus low moisture content), and gives the oldest confirmed honey remains as residue on clay vessels in a tomb in Georgia, dated between 4,700 and 5,500 years, alongside the ancient Georgian custom of burying different honey types with the dead.
